opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I didn't treat GPA as something to maximize for its own sake. Early on, in my first year or so, I did put real effort into coursework, partly because everyone around me was doing that and partly because I wanted to keep my options open. A decent GPA is a kind of baseline: it gets you past certain filters for grad school applications or exchange programs. But once I was above that bar, the marginal return of pushing from, say, very good to near-perfect seemed pretty low compared to what else I could do with that time.

So my rough rule was: make sure the GPA is good enough that it never becomes the reason someone rejects you, and then spend the rest of your energy on things that actually differentiate you. For me that meant writing code, doing research, and building projects that people could use. If you look at what admissions committees or employers in this field care about, a strong project or a meaningful contribution says far more about you than an extra 0.1 on your GPA.

There's also a mindset piece. Many students at top universities are very competitive about grades, and it's easy to get sucked into that and feel anxious if you're not at the top of the ranking. At some point I just accepted that I wouldn't be the best at every course, and that was fine. Some courses I cared about deeply and studied hard because I found them useful. Others I did just enough to get through. Being selective like that freed up a lot of time.

If I were advising an undergrad now, I'd say figure out the threshold that matters for your goals, clear it comfortably, and then invest the rest of your time in something you're genuinely excited about and can show to the world. That compounds much more than grades do.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes targeting a GPA threshold and redirecting effort once above it, but does not clearly say Jiayi invested only the minimum time needed to reach her chosen GPA standard.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I didn't treat it as one big decision. It was more like a running calculation I kept redoing every semester.

Early on, in my first year at Tsinghua, I did care a lot about grades. Partly that was just momentum from the gaokao mindset, where the score is everything. But pretty quickly I noticed something: the courses where I was learning the most were not always the ones where I got the highest grades, and the hours I spent grinding for the last few points in a course often had very low return. Going from a 90 to a 95 in some required class took way more effort than it was worth, and nobody downstream ever asked me about it.

So the rule I settled on was roughly this. Keep the GPA above the threshold where it stops being a filter. For grad school applications, for internships, there is a line below which people won't look at you, and above which they mostly stop caring and look at what you've actually built. Figure out where that line is, stay comfortably above it, and then put every remaining hour into things that compound: research, open source, real projects.

For me that meant I spent a lot of time on reinforcement learning side projects, on building things like Tianshou, instead of optimizing every exam. And in hindsight that was the right trade. When I interviewed, nobody asked about my grade in some elective. They asked about the code, about design decisions, about what went wrong and how I fixed it.

The one caveat I'd add is that this only works if you're actually honest with yourself about the threshold. "I don't care about GPA" is sometimes just a way of avoiding hard courses. The point isn't to care less, it's to care precisely, and to spend the surplus on something that leaves a trace.

r001.rationale: The response recommends keeping GPA comfortably above an external threshold and using remaining time elsewhere, but it does not say Jiayi invested only the minimum time needed to reach a personally chosen GPA standard.

astra-6.text: For me, it was about thinking about what the GPA would help me do next. If I wanted to keep graduate school as an option, then I needed to take it seriously. But I also didn’t want to spend all my time chasing a slightly higher number and miss opportunities to explore my interests. So I’d ask myself: am I spending this extra time actually learning something, or just trying to get a few more points? That was the balance I was trying to find.
